channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: India said trade talks won it the lower tier of the new US tariffs (an extra 10%), even as its USD 190 billion textile industry split over the impact, while New Delhi lined up an INR 800 billion deepwater-energy package and an import-substitution drive.
item.description:
India's commerce ministry said talks with Washington placed the country in the lower band of the new Section 301 tariffs — an additional 10% rather than 12.5% — though exporters remain worried, and the USD 190 billion textile-and-apparel sector is divided, with some fearing lost orders and pressing for a faster trade pact. Against that external pressure, India is doubling down on self-reliance: the petroleum ministry is drawing up an INR 800 billion (roughly USD 9.5 billion) incentive package, covering up to half of exploration costs, to attract foreign investment into deepwater oil and gas. Analysts argue the wider push to cut import dependence — across energy, electronics and materials — is a structural, multi-year investment opportunity rather than a short-term policy gesture. Flooding at Tata Motors' Gujarat plant (see the force-majeure insight in this alert) is a reminder of the domestic risks alongside the opportunity.

Industry Impact

India is the clearest structural growth story for chemical demand, and its import-substitution drive — building domestic energy, electronics and materials capacity — expands the industrial base that consumes adhesives, coatings and sealants while also inviting foreign investment into it. The deepwater energy push, if funded, supports domestic feedstock and construction activity. For producers weighing capacity outside a contracting Europe, India's mix of tariff resilience and self-reliance spending keeps it near the top of the list.

Business Standard | The Hindu Business Line | The Economic Times | The Economic Times | LiveMint

item.title: Emerging-market equity funds led global inflows, Indonesia posted solid growth, and the IMF's chief hailed Argentina's "much sounder" economy under Milei — a broadly resilient picture, though Bangladesh's outlook was cut on banking and energy risks.
item.description:
Global emerging-market equity funds turned to net inflows of USD 1.93 billion in the week to 22 July, topping all markets, as investors looked past Middle East risk. Indonesia's economy grew 5.11% in 2025 and 5.61% in the first quarter of 2026, with household consumption the main driver, though analysts flag a shrinking middle class as a longer-term concern. In Argentina, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva met President Milei and his economy team in Buenos Aires and praised the country's "much sounder" economic standing since 2023 — a notable endorsement for a top IMF debtor. Not all news was positive: S&P cut Bangladesh's outlook to negative, citing a weak banking sector, high energy costs from the Middle East war, and garment-export uncertainty.

Industry Impact

Emerging markets are the main growth frontier for chemical demand, and steady inflows plus Indonesian and Argentine stabilisation support construction, packaging and manufacturing consumption in those markets. The Bangladesh downgrade is a reminder that energy-import-dependent, garment-reliant economies remain fragile to the same oil and trade shocks. For suppliers weighing where to add capacity outside a slow Europe, the ASEAN and Latin American resilience stories keep those regions attractive.

Commercial Times | Kompas | La Nacion | Japan Today | Business Recorder

item.title: A wildfire near Bordeaux severed the rail line to Spain, France warned its drought damage will top 2022's EUR 5.6 billion, a tornado struck a north German town, and floods halted Tata Motors' Gujarat plant — a fresh wave of force majeure.
item.description:
The Atlantic-coast wildfire threatening Bordeaux kept advancing, fully cutting rail traffic south of the city and severing a key Basque-country link to Spain, with an economist warning that large or prolonged fires damage economy, infrastructure and tourism. France's ecological-transition minister said the cost of this year's historic drought will exceed the EUR 5.6 billion recorded in 2022. In Germany, a tornado damaged up to 50 buildings in the Schleswig-Holstein town of Glückstadt. In India, flooding from heavy rain severely disrupted Tata Motors' Sanand plant in Gujarat and supplier facilities, hitting output of the Nexon and Sierra models. And in Canada, British Columbia's Thompson-Nicola district issued evacuation alerts as wildfires advanced. The cluster underlines how routine climate disruption to transport and production has become.

Industry Impact

Each event carries the now-familiar double read for the chemicals industry: near-term disruption to logistics and production (a severed French rail corridor, a halted Indian car plant), and a longer structural pull toward fire-resistant, heat- and weather-resilient coatings, sealants and infrastructure-protection materials as reconstruction recurs. The French rail cut and Gujarat flooding are concrete reminders that supply-chain and customer-site continuity now has a standing weather risk that belongs in planning, not the tail.

La Vanguardia | Anadolu Agency | Le Figaro | Der Standard | Business Standard | The Globe and Mail

item.title: The US House passed a defence bill barring Chinese-linked humanoid robots and lawmakers introduced an AI-oversight bill, while China warned of countermeasures over threatened AI-firm sanctions and memory-maker CXMT raised over USD 8 billion to expand.
item.description:
The National Defence Authorisation Act, passed by the House, prohibits the Pentagon from operating, leasing or procuring humanoid robots linked to "foreign adversaries" — squarely aimed at China's world-leading humanoid sector. Separately, Representatives Obernolte and Trahan formally introduced bipartisan legislation to give the government more oversight of advanced AI models, following last week's "AI kill switch" proposal. China's Commerce Ministry warned of countermeasures after Washington threatened trade restrictions and sanctions on Chinese AI firms over allegations that Moonshot's Kimi model was distilled from a US model. Underlining that the chip race runs both ways, Chinese memory maker CXMT raised more than USD 8 billion to expand — targeting 350,000 wafers a month by end-2026 — and Goldman Sachs expects China's DRAM capacity to double by 2030. The World AI Conference in Shanghai, meanwhile, launched a global AI-governance body.

Industry Impact

The hardening tech split pushes toward two separate technology stacks, which complicates any global producer's plan to standardise plant automation and digital systems across US and Chinese sites. China's memory-capacity surge and robot leadership expand demand for the specialty chemicals, adhesives and thermal materials that go into chips and robots — increasingly on Chinese terms. Expect automation and sourcing strategy to be planned per bloc rather than globally.

SCMP | POLITICO | The Times of India | Corriere della Sera | Commercial Times | Xinhua Daily

item.title: North American firm REalloys is rebuilding a domestic rare-earth supply chain to counter China's export curbs, and the US and Canada are funding critical-minerals self-sufficiency — though industry warns it cannot meet Washington's 2027 deadline.
item.description:
REalloys has spent two years assembling heavy-rare-earth feedstock, separation, metallization and alloying capacity across North America — an attempt to reconstruct a supply chain China dominates. It is part of a broader push: Washington has invested tens of billions across nearly 150 minerals companies to loosen China's grip, and the US and Canada are jointly funding North American supply chains, with a regulatory catalyst from Europe's raw-materials rules. But the effort collides with reality — industry sources say US processing cannot realistically meet Trump's 2027 target to end reliance on Chinese critical minerals, so Washington may have to keep allowing Chinese material in the interim. The stakes are large: the IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook warns of severe economic-security risks from price spikes and trade restrictions in these supply chains.

Industry Impact

Rare earths and critical minerals underpin catalysts, pigments, battery materials and specialty additives across the chemicals sector, so the reshoring drive matters for both supply security and cost. A build-out reduces long-term dependence on Chinese processing but will be slower and pricier than the current supply, meaning higher input costs before relief arrives. Producers with exposure to these inputs should plan for a multi-year transition with continued Chinese supply in the gap.

MarketScreener | MarketScreener | Wallstreet:online | Vietnam News

item.title: Spain has become the main entry point for Chinese carmakers into Europe, with over half a dozen assembly projects, while Audi cut its full-year guidance on a worsening China market — the two-way squeeze on Europe's auto industry.
item.description:
Spain has drawn a cluster of Chinese vehicle-assembly projects, positioning itself as the bridgehead for brands like BYD and Chery to build inside the EU tariff wall and reshape where European cars are made. At the same time, Volkswagen's Audi lowered its 2026 outlook, blaming a deteriorating China market and Middle East tensions — a fresh signal of how German premium brands are being squeezed in their largest market. The electrification backdrop is accelerating: battery-electric vehicles hit 22% of the European new-car market in the first half (up 5 points), and in the US 24% of second-quarter light-vehicle sales were electric or hybrid. Chery, whose LEPAS brand is expanding globally, has now passed 20 million cumulative sales. Thailand, meanwhile, cut its 2026 production target to 1.45 million units as Chinese EV competition bites.

Industry Impact

Autos are a major end-market for structural adhesives, sealants and coatings, and the shift of production toward Chinese-owned plants in Spain redraws where that demand sits and who specifies materials — advantaging suppliers with a footprint near the new Iberian assembly base. Audi's warning and Thailand's cut show legacy volumes eroding, while the EV share gain keeps favouring battery-bonding and lightweighting chemistries over traditional applications. The customer map is fragmenting along the China-versus-incumbent divide.

La Vanguardia | MarketScreener | Wirtschaftswoche | EIA | The Nation

item.title: The Ifo institute's expectations index rose again to 86.7, a third straight monthly improvement, and Chancellor Merz will host an October summit to court international investors — tentative optimism set against Germany's persistent structural strains.
item.description:
Ifo's expectations gauge climbed from a revised 84.3 to 86.7, beating forecasts and suggesting firms see the worst passing despite the Iran war. Building on that, Merz is planning a Berlin summit in October — a "Choose Germany" style pitch — to attract international investment and revive years of sluggish growth, following his recent cabinet reshuffle. But the structural problems remain stark: German workers took an average of 22 sick days in 2024, among the highest internationally and a drag on output; the skilled-labour shortage is acute (an AfD candidate in Saxony-Anhalt controversially insists it be solved "without immigration"); and the reshuffle itself drew criticism, with a dismissed health-ministry official publicly rebuking Merz. The picture is a fragile confidence recovery layered over unresolved competitiveness problems.

Industry Impact

Germany is the heart of European chemical and industrial demand, so a genuine confidence turn — if sustained — would support the construction and manufacturing volumes that drive adhesives, coatings and sealants. But the sick-leave and skilled-labour data explain why producers keep flagging Germany as a high-cost, low-flexibility base (echoing the East German investment-cut survey from recent alerts). An investor summit signals intent; the demand recovery it implies is still unproven.

Financial Post | Le Figaro | MarketScreener | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Süddeutsche Zeitung

item.title: The EU is implementing a Forced Labour Regulation that will bar goods made with forced labour from December 2027, while Russia asked the WTO for a dispute panel over the EU's carbon border levy — Europe's trade-defence agenda drawing pushback.
item.description:
The Forced Labour Regulation (FLR) takes full effect on 14 December 2027 and will ban products made wholly or partly with forced labour from the EU market, adding a due-diligence and traceability burden for anyone selling into Europe — a mirror image of the forced-labour justification the US used for its own tariffs. Separately, Russia formally requested a WTO dispute panel over the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and Emissions Trading System, arguing they are disguised trade barriers — the first formal WTO challenge to CBAM as it moves toward charging importers for embedded carbon. Turkey, meanwhile, says it is negotiating continuously against the EU's "wave of protectionism," and Michelin welcomed the EU's 24.4–45.3% anti-dumping duties on Chinese tyres as a way to end price dumping. Together these show Europe simultaneously tightening market access and defending its measures internationally.

Industry Impact

Both measures reach the chemicals value chain. CBAM will eventually price the carbon embedded in imported chemicals, steel and other inputs, raising costs and paperwork for anyone shipping into the EU — and a WTO challenge introduces uncertainty over how far it will stand. The FLR adds supply-chain due-diligence obligations on raw materials. For an EU-based producer, CBAM can be a competitive shield against high-carbon imports; for a global one, both rules raise the compliance cost of serving the European market.

The Nation | WTO | Le Figaro | Dünya

item.title: A German Fraunhofer lab developed a way to seal paper packaging without adhesive, a court widened packaging-recycling liability to reusable bags, and wienerberger backed the EU's ETS reform — signs of where materials regulation is heading.
item.description:
Fraunhofer's PAPURE project (closing September 2026) uses laser heating to bond paper packaging without glue, aiming to make paper packaging fully recyclable and to displace plastic layers — a direct challenge and opportunity for the adhesives that currently seal packaging. In parallel, Germany's Federal Administrative Court in Leipzig ruled that sturdy reusable plastic carrier bags count as "packaging" under the Dual System, making retailers liable for recycling fees and reinforcing the producer-responsibility trend that increasingly dictates packaging design. Building-materials maker wienerberger publicly welcomed the European Commission's ETS proposals as a step to protect industrial competitiveness, a rare industry endorsement of a green-policy revision. Around these, the circular economy keeps advancing — France's used-auto-parts market is professionalising around data and traceability — while Russian specialty-chemicals maker OKSIDE warns of continued import dependence in low-tonnage chemicals.

Industry Impact

This is the core so-what for adhesives, coatings and sealants: recyclability is becoming a design constraint, and adhesive-free sealing (if it scales) threatens a traditional application even as it opens demand for new functional coatings and bio-based bonding. Wider producer-responsibility liability raises customers' incentive to switch to easily recyclable, mono-material packaging — favouring suppliers who can offer debondable or compatible adhesive systems. Producers that treat circularity as a product-development driver, not a compliance cost, stand to gain share.

BBC News | FAZ | MarketScreener | Challenges

item.title: Profits at China's industrial firms rose 18.7% year-on-year to CNY 3.95 trillion in the first half, led by high-tech sectors, as trade topped CNY 25 trillion and analysts described China as the world's undisputed industrial power.
item.description:
The profit surge — even with automakers' profits down 19.5% and mining weak — shows the strength concentrating in high-value manufacturing. Reinforcing the picture, China's first-half imports and exports surpassed CNY 25 trillion for the first time, robot exports rose 18.6% (shipped to 141 countries) and power-and-storage battery exports climbed 42.5%. An ABC analysis went further, arguing China has become the undisputed leader of global industrial production in just 35 years, with near-total dominance of mineral refining and manufacturing scale — a structural advantage the West is struggling to counter (see the rare-earth insight in this alert). The MIIT says China's high-end emerging-industry competitiveness keeps rising. The one soft spot is the domestic-demand brake visible in the carmakers' profit slump, which is why Beijing keeps signalling stimulus.

Industry Impact

China's industrial dominance cuts two ways for a chemicals group: it is the largest and fastest-innovating customer base and a source of low-cost inputs, but also an increasingly formidable competitor moving up the value chain into specialty materials. The battery and robot export surges expand demand for the adhesives, thermal materials and coatings that go into them — much of it now specified by Chinese producers. The weak auto profits are a caution that Chinese end-demand is uneven, not uniformly booming.

Dünya | ABC Australia | Xinhua Daily | China Economic Net | Xinhua Daily | Xinhua Daily

item.title: The Monetary Authority of Singapore unexpectedly tightened policy a second time in three months to contain war-driven inflation, letting its currency rise faster, even as monitor AMRO raised the city-state's 2026 growth forecast to 4.8%.
item.description:
The move caught markets off guard — Bank of America had expected no change — and the Singapore dollar strengthened past 1.29 per US dollar. MAS, which manages policy through the exchange rate rather than interest rates, steepened the currency's appreciation path (though by less than in April) and warned inflation will stay elevated into early 2027, driven by volatile energy prices from the Middle East conflict. The tightening sits against a strikingly strong economy: AMRO lifted Singapore's 2026 growth forecast from 3.4% to 4.8% on AI-driven demand, June manufacturing output rose 7.2% year-on-year (9.6% excluding biomedical), and second-quarter GDP grew 5.7%. MAS added that even a renewed Middle East escalation is not expected to worsen the impact on Singapore materially, having judged the recent oil spike as milder than April's.

Industry Impact

Singapore is a major petrochemical and specialty-chemicals hub (Jurong Island) and a bellwether for Asian trade, so a central bank tightening into strength signals that regional inflation — not weakness — is the near-term risk. A stronger Singapore dollar raises costs for dollar-priced feedstock imports but supports purchasing power. The AI-driven manufacturing surge is a demand positive for electronics-linked adhesives and encapsulants routed through the region.

MarketScreener | New Indian Express | Lianhe Zaobao | CNA | Lianhe Zaobao | Singapore Business Review

item.title: The Fed (30 July), Bank of England and Bank of Japan all set rates this week in an unusually hard-to-call round, while the IMF cut its 2026 global growth forecast, blaming the US-led trade war and the Middle East conflict.
item.description:
The Fed is the focus: most economists, including Deutsche Bank and Bank of America, still expect no change, but the odds of a September hike are rising and markets want to know whether new Chair Kevin Warsh signals one — "three shocks" (the war, tariffs and a firm economy) have made the call genuinely uncertain, and a small number of officials may even dissent toward a hike. The Bank of England is expected to hold at 3.75% for a fourth straight meeting while warning it may still need to move if energy prices rebound; the Bank of Japan also decides, and Pakistan's central bank has already held at 11.5%. Framing all of this, the IMF lowered its 2026 world growth forecast, citing Trump's trade war and the wars as a drag — the latest in a string of downgrades this year. The oil drop (see other insight in this alert) has, at least briefly, taken some pressure off the inflation side of these decisions.

Industry Impact

Rates staying higher for longer keeps financing costs elevated for the construction and durable-goods demand that drives adhesives, coatings and sealants volumes. A Fed that even hints at hiking would lift the dollar and squeeze emerging-market customers; a hold plus falling oil would be the friendlier outcome. The IMF downgrade confirms a soft demand backdrop into 2027, reinforcing a "defend margins, don't count on a rebound" posture for industrial suppliers.

Commercial Times | Commercial Times | Cnyes | MarketScreener | Hong Kong Economic Times | La Presse

item.title: A pause in US strikes on Iran dropped Brent crude almost 9% to under USD 88, unwinding much of the war premium, lifting shares, bonds and gold, and easing the inflation fears that had gripped markets for weeks.
item.description:
The reversal is sharp: only days ago Brent was near USD 100 and the US was enforcing a naval blockade of Iran's ports with live fire. On 27 July a pause in US bombing sent Brent down 8.7% to USD 88.36 and WTI down 7.5%, with Asian shares and bonds rallying and the dollar easing as risk appetite returned. The de-escalation is partial and fragile — a New York Times analysis describes Trump as "increasingly frustrated and erratic," his plan to topple Iran's leadership having stalled — and the conflict is still widening at the edges: Ukrainian drones struck an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea and Saudi jets hit Houthi sites in Yemen. Markets are treating the pause as real for now: gold rose as inflation worries cooled, and analysts say oil and the Fed decision will drive sentiment this week. Whether the calm holds depends on a durable ceasefire that has not yet been agreed.

Industry Impact

For chemical producers this is direct relief: Brent back below USD 90 pulls down petrochemical feedstock, energy and freight costs that had been squeezing margins on adhesives, coatings and sealants. Lower oil also eases the inflation pressure that was pushing central banks toward tightening. But the pause is not a settlement — the same volatility that spiked prices could return quickly — so it argues for treating the relief as a window, not a new baseline, when hedging feedstock and freight.

Le Figaro | Pakistan Today | MarketScreener | Cnyes | The Straits Times | Yahoo Taiwan
